scenes.text: They set this machine in front of me and asked what I remember. Child, I am one hundred and six years old. Memory is near all I own, and it don't sit quiet. Lean in close now. Let me tell you about the world we built.

scenes.text: Greenwood. Thirty-five square blocks on the north side of Tulsa, Oklahoma. Ten thousand of us. White folks took to calling it Black Wall Street. We just called it ours.
We had the Stradford, finest colored-owned hotel in America. The Dreamland Theatre, seven hundred fifty seats and a piano that never slept. Doctors, lawyers, two newspapers of our own.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, church congregation pouring out, families in Sunday best
scenes.text: A dollar came into Greenwood and stayed, passing hand to hand to hand before it ever left. That wasn't luck, sugar. That was a people agreeing on what they were worth.

My daddy was Dr. Ambrose Freeman. Office up a narrow stair on Greenwood Avenue, his name painted gold on the glass. Mama was his nurse when she wasn't being my mother — which she'd tell you was the harder job.

I was eight that spring. Sunday dresses, penny candy, patent-leather shoes. In the one photograph we saved, somebody tinted my ribbon pink by hand. I remember that ribbon better than some whole years.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, children playing in a dirt lot, jump rope, wagons
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, children playing in a dirt lot, jump rope, wagons
scenes.text: Daddy used to say Greenwood was a thought before it was a town. Imagination is the workshop, Opal. Everything out here got built twice — once inside somebody, once in the brick.
We had our own schools too. Booker T. Washington High stood up on that hill like it knew something. We were not waiting on anybody's permission to be somebody. We already were.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, Memorial Day parade, flags, marching veterans, 1921
scenes.text: Monday, May thirtieth, 1921. Memorial Day. Flags all down Main Street, veterans marching, most stores shut. The parade was downtown — the white part of town — but a workday don't stop for everybody.
Dick Rowland was nineteen. Shined shoes on Main. Folks called him Diamond Dick. I knew his grin the way a child knows grown folks — by the kindness or the lack of it. His was kindness.
Jim Crow did its arithmetic on him daily. The only washroom a colored man could use downtown sat at the top of the Drexel Building. To reach it, you rode the elevator. That is all that boy was doing.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, downtown Tulsa street, streetcars and awnings
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, downtown Tulsa street, streetcars and awnings
scenes.text: The elevator girl was Sarah Page, seventeen, white, working her shift same as any Monday. Two young people in a box of brass and cable. History has squeezed into smaller rooms than that, child. Not many.
The car lurched. He stumbled. His hand caught her arm the way you would catch anybody's arm. She hollered. He ran — because a colored boy in 1921 knew exactly what a holler could cost him.
A clerk from the store next door heard the scream, saw a Black boy running, and let his imagination finish the story. Fear writes fast, child. Faster than truth can lace its shoes.

scenes.text: Now here is what nobody led with: the police who talked to Sarah Page didn't smell much fire in it. No charge she would swear to. The detectives shrugged. On any honest day, that is where it ends.

scenes.text: That night we slept easy under our own roofs, in the town we built twice. I have spent a hundred years learning how precious an easy sleep is, child. That was the last one for a long while.

Tuesday morning, May thirty-first, they arrested Dick anyway, quiet, and set him in the courthouse jail. Sheriff Willard McCullough held the keys. Remember his name. Goodness wore every color that week.

scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, Greenwood evening street life, storefront lamps
scenes.text: Greenwood didn't know one thing about it yet. Supper smells drifting, the Dreamland piano warming up, men sweeping their own storefronts. We were rich in the way that counts — we belonged to each other.
But downtown, an afternoon paper needed selling. The Tulsa Tribune. And there is no cheaper fuel on God's green earth than a white woman's scream and a Black man's name.
They set it in type: NAB NEGRO FOR ATTACKING GIRL IN AN ELEVATOR. Eight words, most of them seasoning on a story that had no meat. A match, child, dipped in ink.

scenes.text: And deeper in that paper, folks swore, an invitation to a lynching, printed plain. Go look for it today. That page is torn out of every archive by somebody's careful hand. Paper burns, baby. Witness don't.

scenes.text: A little after three, the Tribune hit the street. Newsboys hollering that headline on every corner downtown. Folks said you could stand on our side of the tracks and feel it coming. Like weather.
By suppertime, white Tulsa had chewed that story down to one word: rope. A mob had lynched a white boy in this same town not a year before, and the law just watched. Everybody knew the recipe worked.

scenes.text: By seven-thirty they were collecting outside the courthouse. Hundreds, then more. McCullough barred the doors, killed the elevator, put riflemen on the stairs. The mob asked for Dick Rowland. The sheriff said no.

Down on Greenwood, men who had worn this country's uniform in France set down their suppers and stood up. If the law could not hold that line, they would. Not rage, child. Arithmetic. They knew what mobs do.

scenes.text: Daddy locked the office early. Mama held my hand too tight, and the air had changed — you could taste tomorrow in it, like copper. Next time I'll tell you how one gun went off and the whole world tore its shirt.

This is Black Wall Street, part one of ten. I'm telling the whole story, child — every part of it, right here on this channel. Go on and find part two. The night I lost my easy sleep is waiting on you.
